final.title: Human-in-the-loop is a clear approval boundary
final.body:
If you are rethinking human-in-the-loop design, do not start with the model. Start with one recurring workflow and ask a simpler question: which decision must stay with you before the output can take effect? That is the control boundary.

In a small business, the useful split is not “AI or no AI.” It is filter, route, or approve. AI can sort, extract, or draft. Human approval stays where the consequence is real: money movement, customer commitments, legal or financial risk, or anything that does not fit a simple template.

That is also how Bareni’s own demos are meant to be read. In the accounts-payable demo, payment blocking and human-only approval are part of the design; the blocked payment is a manual simulation on synthetic data. In the knowledge assistant demo, sources are shown so the answer stays grounded instead of guessed. Both are examples of how approval gates work in design, not customer results.

For an owner-operator, the next step is plain: pick one recurring workflow and write the approval rule in one sentence. For example: “AI may draft or flag this item, but I approve anything that moves money or changes a commitment.” If you cannot write that sentence cleanly, the workflow is not ready yet. Human-in-the-loop is just that: the system does the repetitive checking, and you keep the last gate when the decision matters.

final.title: Human-in-the-loop is a control boundary, not a slogan
final.body:
If you are rethinking human-in-the-loop design, start with one recurring workflow and ask a plain question: which decision must stay with you before the output can take effect? That is the control boundary. In a small business, the useful split is usually filter, route, or approve. AI can sort, extract, or draft. Human approval stays where the consequence is real: money movement, customer commitments, legal or financial risk, or anything outside a simple template.

That boundary matters because a wrong automated decision can be expensive, while a review step is only friction. The point is not to force AI into every task. It is to use it where it helps the repetitive checking, and keep the last gate human where judgment still matters.

We built two self-contained demos that show the pattern, not customer results. In the accounts-payable demo, payment blocking and human-only approval are part of the design; the blocked payment is a manual simulation on synthetic data. In the knowledge assistant demo, sources are shown so the answer is grounded instead of guessed. Both are examples of how approval gates work in design, not proof of production use.

A practical next step is to write one sentence for a workflow you repeat often: “AI may draft or flag this item, but I approve anything that moves money or changes a commitment.” If you cannot write that sentence cleanly, the workflow is not ready for automation yet. That is usually where the trouble starts. The spreadsheet does enjoy an opinion.
